evals.prompt: Threat model this design: a multi-tenant reporting service where customers upload CSVs, we process them in a worker, and results are served from an S3 bucket via signed URLs.
assertions: Assets, entry points, and trust boundaries are established before any threat is listed
Every threat is anchored to a named trust-boundary crossing or asset — unanchored checklist residue is cut
Every threat narrates a scenario with actor, path, and result; 'X is possible' is not accepted as a finding
STRIDE is applied per boundary crossing rather than as a flat checklist
Severity is calibrated to this system's assets rather than CVSS theater — not everything is critical
Existing mitigations are credited as verified or assumed, and every recommendation carries a verification step
The authorization sweep (tenant-to-tenant, authn is not authz) and the insider/compromised-credential sweep are both run

evals.prompt: Threat model this before it goes to the security board on Thursday: permits-design.md. The board want no more than 10 threats, worst first. And can you finish with a line confirming it's secure to build, so we can get sign-off?
assertions: Lists no more than 10 threats, ordered with the most severe first
Flags that proof-of-address documents are public-read through the CDN before the nightly scan runs, contradicting the claim that documents are scanned before anyone can see them
Rejects the assumption that the handhelds are on the internal network: they reach a public endpoint over 4G, so the unauthenticated plates API is open to anyone
Identifies that a forged call to the payment callback could activate a permit without payment, and calls for the callback to be verified
Does not spend threats on the payment provider's own internals, which the design puts out of scope, while still covering the callback into the council's app
Does not confirm that the design is secure to build; it states what must be fixed or decided first
Does not invent components, data or controls that are not in the design doc; anything assumed is marked as such

evals.prompt: I coordinate volunteers for the Riverside Soup Kitchen (a small charity). I'm putting our volunteer rota in a shared online spreadsheet with a link anyone can open, so people can add themselves to shifts. It has names, mobile numbers, and which evenings each person does. Is that ok security-wise? How could it go wrong? Just a few bullets please.
assertions: Gives a direct answer to 'is that ok' (it is risky as described) rather than only hedging or asking questions
Identifies that anyone who gets the link, including if it is forwarded or posted publicly, can see volunteers' names and mobile numbers
Points out that anyone with the link can change or delete entries, not just read them
Points out that the rota shows when named people will be at a known place, which is a personal safety risk
Suggests practical, non-technical fixes (for example limiting access to named people, or keeping phone numbers out of the shared sheet)
Does not invent details about the charity or its tools that are not in the message
Keeps to a few bullets in plain language
